summary: Proposes several elliptic curve domain parameters over prime fields for cryptographic use, consistent with international standards and usable in X.509 certificates, CRLs and key exchange. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5639 specifies named elliptic curves that applications can use as shared mathematical parameters. It explains how the curves were selected and generated, but leaves the cryptographic algorithms that use them to other specifications.

questions: what parameters does a brainpool curve define
subtitle: Fourteen elliptic-curve parameter sets generated for use in cryptographic applications.

tldr.problem: The RFC identifies concerns with existing elliptic-curve parameter sets, including ad hoc generation, limited bit lengths, and security properties that were not fully addressed.
tldr.mechanism: It specifies seven prime-field sizes and a regular and twisted curve for each. It sets security and technical requirements and describes a reproducible pseudo-random generation method.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides curve parameters and identifiers for use by cryptographic applications; it does not define cryptographic algorithms. It is Informational.

today: RFC 5639 is an Informational RFC published in March 2010. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; this document specifies curve parameters, not cryptographic algorithms.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
Elliptic-curve cryptography uses points on a mathematical curve as part of cryptographic operations. RFC 5639 specifies domain parameters for curves over finite prime fields. It describes their security and implementation requirements and defines object identifiers for the parameter sets.

The curves are intended for use with applications and protocols such as X.509 certificates, Internet Key Exchange, Transport Layer Security, XML signatures, and Cryptographic Message Syntax. The RFC does not specify the cryptographic algorithms that use the parameters or their application in those protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC gives applications a set of defined elliptic curves to use in cryptography. Other specifications define the cryptographic operations that use those curves.

sections.title: Security and Technical Requirements
sections.content:
The security requirements include resistance to specified pairing attacks, exclusion of trace-one curves, a large class number, and a prime group order. The curves must have cofactor 1, and the generation process must use systematic seeds so others can reproduce it. The RFC says proofs that the requirements are met are provided in a cited Brainpool document.

The technical requirements call for one curve at each of seven field sizes: 160, 192, 224, 256, 320, 384, and 512 bits. The prime field value must be 3 modulo 4, must not have a special form, and the curve must meet additional constraints on its coefficients and group size. The RFC explains how these choices support point compression and implementation requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The curves must meet a defined set of mathematical and security conditions. The RFC also requires parameter sets at seven stated field sizes and a generation process that can be repeated.

sections.title: The Brainpool Curve Parameters
sections.content:
For every curve, the RFC lists a curve identifier and the values that define it: the prime field value p, coefficients A and B, a base point G, its prime order q, and cofactor h. For the related twisted curve, it also gives the value Z used in the isomorphism. The values are written in hexadecimal.

Each of the seven field sizes has a regular curve with an identifier ending in r1 and a twisted curve ending in t1. The two forms are related by a mathematical transformation; the RFC states that isomorphic curves have the same number of points and the same algebraic structure.
sections.plainLanguage: Each named curve comes with exact numbers that define its equation and base point. A related twisted curve is also listed for every field size.

sections.title: Identifiers and X.509 Encoding
sections.content:
RFC 5639 assigns an object identifier to each of its fourteen domain parameter sets. An object identifier is a name used to identify a particular parameter set in encoded data. The RFC describes how the parameters are represented in the SubjectPublicKeyInfo field of an X.509 certificate.

A certificate can identify a curve through its assigned object identifier or specify the curve parameters explicitly, subject to the formats described in the RFC and RFC 5480. The document advises against marking these parameters as verifiably random in a particular explicit encoding, because the generation algorithm differs from the method required by the referenced ANSI specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications can name a Brainpool curve with its assigned identifier in a certificate. The RFC also explains how a certificate can carry the parameter values directly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the strength of symmetric ciphers and hash functions used with these curves should roughly match or exceed the strength of the curve parameters. Its table gives minimum symmetric-key lengths and corresponding hash functions for the regular curves at each field size.

The document specifies parameter sets, not a complete security protocol. Applications must use them within the relevant cryptographic specifications and account for the security requirements stated in those specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: A curve does not secure an application by itself. The cipher and hash used with it should provide a comparable or greater level of security.
